title: Ancient Romans Marked Places Struck by Lightning
mediaSource: Hadrian Villa lightning inscription Fulgur Submanium Roman ritual archaeology

scenes.title: Romans did not ignore a lightning strike
scenes.narration: At Hadrian's Villa in Italy archaeologists found a marble inscription linked to a place believed to have been struck by lightning.

scenes.title: The inscription invoked a god of night lightning
scenes.narration: The carved words refer to Summanus, a Roman deity associated with lightning at night.

scenes.title: Lightning could make a place sacred
scenes.narration: Romans sometimes treated lightning-struck places or objects as signs that the divine had entered the human world.

scenes.title: Struck objects could even be buried
scenes.narration: Researchers think the inscription may relate to a ritual in which lightning-struck objects were buried and the location was formally set apart.

scenes.title: A tiny sign reveals a whole ritual system
scenes.narration: The slab offers rare physical evidence for how Romans interpreted a natural event and then changed the meaning of the space around it.

scenes.title: One lightning strike could transform a place
scenes.narration: To us it is weather. To ancient Romans a lightning strike could turn an ordinary location into sacred ground.
